question: Whether familiarity-based recognition is impaired in (amnestic) MCI relative to healthy older adults, measured with behavioural recognition paradigms. Both papers address it: P-632 compares 24 aMCI with 24 matched older controls, and P-667 compares 26 MCI with 40 older adults, plus 40 young adults. The channel matches (cognitive testing). The paradigms differ (process dissociation, frequency judgments and lifetime familiarity against boundary-extension ROC); the rule allows this.
metric: Direction of the group difference in both papers: F tests in P-632, Kruskal-Wallis tests with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc contrasts (alpha 0.017) in P-667. Neither paper prints effect-size intervals.

figures.P-632: PDP familiarity, aMCI against older controls: F(1,45) < 1, no difference. Frequency judgments after recent exposure: lower correlation in aMCI, F(1,45) = 18.91, p < .001, a familiarity deficit. Lifetime familiarity for object concepts: no difference.
figures.P-667: ROC familiarity medians: YA 0.64, OA 0.37, MCI -0.25; three-group Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.002. In post hoc tests only YA against MCI is significant (p = 0.001, r = 0.42), and YA against OA gives p = 0.061. Table 4 marks only 'YA ≠ MCI', so no significant OA-against-MCI difference is reported. The abstract nonetheless says the OA and MCI groups could be differentiated.

matched_figure_check: P-667's OA-against-MCI contrast matches P-632's contrast (MCI against age-matched controls). It is not significant, which agrees with P-632's spared PDP familiarity (F < 1). Where P-632 does find a deficit (frequency judgments of recent exposure), the direction agrees with P-667's lower MCI median. The papers' own matched figures leave no opposite result.
reason: The recorded opposition, familiarity spared (P-632) against impaired (P-667), rests on the record reading P-667's three-group p = 0.002 and its abstract as an MCI-against-older-adults result (condition 6). P-667's printed post hoc tests show a significant deficit only against young adults. Against age-matched controls both papers find no significant difference on a dual-process familiarity estimate, and P-632's frequency-judgment deficit points the same way as P-667's MCI results (condition 3). No opposite significant directions and no intervals are printed, so condition 4 is not met.

quotes.quote: Familiarity was spared on the PDP task, but was impaired when probed with frequency judgments for recently exposed words in aMCI.
Familiarity did not differ between groups, F(1, 45) < 1

Estimates of familiarity were significantly higher among YA participants than among patients with MCI (|ΔRank| = 26.70, p = 0.001, r = 0.42). Differences in estimates of familiarity between YA and OA groups were less pronounced (p = 0.061).
The α level for post hoc tests (Siegel & Castellan, 1988) related to BE was set at 0.017
The OA and MCI groups could be differentiated by the degree of familiarity associated with BE, wherein the latter group displayed minimal familiarity.
